doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Don Ewell, North Carolina college band, Navy and move to New York
summary: Ewell's style, joining a Basie-stock college band at the University of North Carolina, Navy band service, then New York and Manhattan School of Music.

bands.name: University of North Carolina college band

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: a contemporary, what was then contemporary. He used to sound a little like Teddy Wilson and Jess Stacey. That was contemporary when he came up. But then after the war he went back and he became like Jelly Roll Morton. He was not original but he was identifiable. In other words the idea is if you’re going to pick a style to play in, that’s okay, as long as you’re recognizable. Like Scott Hamilton. They thought he was crazy, you know, this kid coming around. In the meantime there’s Coltrane, and here’s this kid sounds like Flip Phillips or Don Byas or whatever, but it’s him, and it sounds like him as opposed to guys who just copy and you don’t know who they are if you go like that. So this little group I used to go sit in with, and the trumpet player took me aside and he taught me chords. I used to go to his house. And then I wound up in the Navy. No first I went to the University of North Carolina and I got in a college band there. It was quite an experience because I used to play in the student lounge, right? You know I’m playing, so these two very imperious, regal looking guys, full of confidence, Wayne Fulton Denning was the trumpet player, and the trombone player’s name was Bud Montgomery. And these guys were terrific. And they had taken over this band which was a pretty well known band in the south. And they asked me if I wanted to join the band. And I said I had zero experience. So I gulped, and I remember hearing, and they used to play Basie stocks. Didn’t have any original arrangements. But see that’s — now they have to pay guys to transcribe this stuff. You could go in the store and buy “Down for Double” and all these great, “Tuesday in Town” all these great arrangements of the 1940s bands. So we used to play those. But when I heard them play it almost blew me off the chair. I didn’t know what the hell I was doing and I had a crash course. I don’t know how I kept the job. And then we used to go around weekends and play all these fancy girls schools. It was a great education. And the guy that played third tenor in the band, a little skinny kid named Bud Shank played in that. Some guys, most of those guys didn’t even wind up being musicians probably. And Bud Montgomery, I remember he played like Urbie Green. He could play like that, I’m not kidding you. There are people you never heard of that do that. Maybe at Hamilton. You don’t know. So that was my early experience. And in the Navy I wound up in the Navy band and I went to the Pacific for a while and all that. And when I got back, instead of going back to the University of North Carolina to get my degree, I had about two and a half years down there before I went in the Navy, I moved to New York, I got married and moved to New York and went to Manhattan School of Music. And who did I find there? Who became my mentor and dearest, dearest friend was John Lewis. Max Roach was there, all the — Juilliard didn’t take them. That business about Miles at Juilliard, I don’t know how that happened with those guys.
